status_summary: The 2026 National Defense Strategy (posted 2026-01-23) keeps a one-war-plus planning model, according to CSIS: the United States plans for one major war, with a second conflict, such as defending Europe against Russia while fighting China, handled largely by allies. CSIS says the strategy acknowledges the simultaneity problem but gives no force size, structure or posture figures, and a Reagan Institute analysis reads it as conceding that the United States cannot plan to fight two major wars at once. No service-by-service two-war scenarios were found in public descriptions.

timeline.event: The Department of War released the 2026 National Defense Strategy, which per CSIS keeps a one-war-plus construct with a second conflict falling largely to allies and gives no force-size figures.

title: Adopt a two-war force-sizing construct with scenarios for each service
uncertainties: The strategy text could not be fetched in this review (the hosting site blocks the research tools); its source entry is copied from c04-08, which read it through a browser retrieval, and the posting date comes from the hosting address. Descriptions of the force-sizing construct come from CSIS (dated 2026-01-27) and the Reagan Institute (dated 2026-07-01), which agree that the strategy does not plan for two simultaneous wars; a Stimson Center analysis, whose page prints no date and is marked undated, says the strategy admits the United States cannot manage concurrent conflicts alone. Diverged is chosen because the stated construct is materially different from a two-war standard; not_started is an alternative if the strategy's silence on force sizing is read as no decision. The classified force-planning guidance is not public. Public Law 119-60 Sec. 364 (report on critical munitions for simultaneous conflicts) was seen only as a title.
